summary: Describes a protocol IBM implemented in many of its SNMP agents to allow dynamic extension of the supported MIBs. It is Experimental and was replaced by RFC 1592.

eli5.summary: It is a way to add new things to a device's report while it is running.

questions: how do you extend an snmp agent
subtitle: Dynamic extension of SNMP agents through sub-agent registration.

tldr.problem: SNMP agents cannot dynamically add or monitor new variables without recompiling the agent, limiting how easily administrators can extend network management capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: SNMP-DPI allows separate sub-agent processes to register with the main SNMP agent, which then forwards relevant queries to them and returns their responses to management stations.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can add custom monitoring variables by writing sub-agents, while remote management stations see a unified agent. RFC 1592 replaced this with improved mechanisms.

today: RFC 1228 is Experimental and is obsoleted by RFC 1592, which provides an improved sub-agent interface based on field experience.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1228 defines the Simple Network Management Protocol Distributed Program Interface (SNMP-DPI), a protocol extension that allows network administrators to dynamically add new management variables to SNMP agents without recompiling them.

SNMP-DPI has been in use at IBM since 1989 and is built into SNMP agents for systems like VM, MVS and OS/2. It works by having separate sub-agent processes register with the main SNMP agent; when remote management stations query for variables managed by a sub-agent, the main agent forwards the request and returns the response transparently.
sections.eli5: Instead of having to rebuild the entire monitoring tool whenever you want to track something new, SNMP-DPI lets you plug in a small helper that the tool automatically asks for the new information.

sections.title: The Extension Problem
sections.content:
SNMP defines a Management Information Base (MIB), a collection of variables that network devices can report. While the MIB has a core set of standard variables, it is designed to be extended. However, conventional SNMP agents provide no way for administrators to add custom variables. For instance, an organization might want to monitor CPU utilization as a percentage, but most agents lack a built-in way to expose such metrics.

SNMP-DPI solves this by providing a lightweight mechanism for a separate process to register itself as managing certain MIB variables with the SNMP agent. When the agent receives a query for one of those variables, it passes the request to the registering process, receives the answer, and packages it into a standard SNMP response back to the management station. Remote managers remain unaware that multiple processes are involved; they see a single cohesive agent.
sections.eli5: The problem is that if you want the monitoring tool to track something it wasn't designed for, you normally have to edit and recompile the whole tool. SNMP-DPI sidesteps this by letting a helper program claim ownership of new information.

sections.title: How SNMP-DPI Works
sections.content:
SNMP-DPI communication happens over a stream connection, typically TCP, between the main SNMP agent and sub-agent processes. A sub-agent begins by registering the set of MIB variables it will manage, then waits for incoming requests. The SNMP agent can initiate three types of requests: GET (retrieve a variable), GET-NEXT (iterate through variables), and SET (modify a variable). In response, the sub-agent returns a RESPONSE packet. A sub-agent can also initiate two operations: REGISTER (to register new variables) and TRAP (to send alert notifications).

To discover the DPI listening port, sub-agents do not need to know SNMP packet encoding. Instead, the DPI provides a simple library routine that generates an SNMP GET request for the agent's port, parses the response, and establishes the connection. This shields sub-agent developers from ASN.1 and SNMP PDU encoding details.
sections.eli5: A helper program connects to the main monitor and says 'I have information about variables X, Y, and Z.' Then when someone asks about those variables, the main monitor passes the question to the helper and sends back the answer.

sections.title: SNMP-DPI Packets
sections.content:
SNMP-DPI packets are sent over the stream connection with a 2-byte length header in network byte order, followed by the packet data. Each packet begins with a 6-byte header: protocol major version, minor version, release number, and packet type. The packet types are GET, GET-NEXT, SET, TRAP, RESPONSE, and REGISTER.

The protocol has been carefully designed to minimize sub-agent complexity. The main SNMP agent handles ASN.1 and SNMP PDU conversion; sub-agents work with simpler DPI packet structures. This design choice makes sub-agent development accessible to administrators unfamiliar with SNMP internals.
sections.eli5: Each message between the helper and the monitor starts with a length, version number, and type of message. This is much simpler than the full SNMP format, so writing the helper is easier.

sections.title: Practical Use and Status
sections.content:
SNMP-DPI enables several deployment scenarios. A sub-agent can run as a separate process on the same host as the agent, or potentially even on a different host via network connection, provided a stream transport is available. Custom sub-agents can monitor application-specific metrics, manage enterprise-specific MIB variables, or extend the agent's capabilities after deployment without downtime.

This protocol is an Experimental RFC as of August 1991 and was succeeded by RFC 1592, which refined the interface based on implementations and lessons learned in the field.
sections.eli5: You can write a small program on your server that feeds custom information to the monitor, and users see those new metrics right alongside the standard ones. Later, a better version of the protocol (RFC 1592) replaced this.
